sections.html:
If your house is inside Denver, its deed and any deed of trust are filed with the Recording Division of the Denver Clerk and Recorder, 200 W. 14th Ave., Denver, CO 80204. Remote service covers most needs, and walk-ins need an appointment. Arrive over ten minutes late and the staff may ask you to reschedule.

Because Denver is a consolidated city and county, the Public Trustee, who runs foreclosures and handles releases of deeds of trust, works for the same government.

A standard document costs $43. Other common charges:

Document or serviceFee
Standard document$43 per document
Certified copy$1 certification plus $0.25 per page
Release of deed of trust$73 total, including a $30 Public Trustee fee
UCC statement, 1 to 2 pages$13
UCC statement, 3 or more pages$18
UCC statement, e-recorded$8
Federal tax lien$43
DD-214 military dischargeFree
Documentary fee on conveyances$0.10 per $1,000, none under $500

Fees are scheduled to rise on July 1 under a new state law, so confirm the current amount with the office before you mail a check.

The only charge that follows the sale price is the documentary fee on real estate grants and conveyances. It is $0.10 per $1,000 of the price, and amounts under $500 owe nothing. Your closing agent calculates it and collects it, so it appears as a line on the settlement statement.

E-recording is the fast route. Denver says mailed documents can take 7 to 10 days, while an e-recorded one goes through in minutes. Your options:

  • E-recording through the approved vendors, EPN and CSC.
  • Mail: the document, a self-addressed envelope and a check or money order payable to Manager of Finance.
  • In person: cash, check, money order or a Mastercard, Visa or Discover card. Temporary checks are not accepted.
  • By phone: the office cannot take card information this way.

Few sellers file anything themselves. The title or escrow company records the deed as part of closing.

A recordable document needs a one-inch top margin and half-inch side margins under C.R.S. 30-10-406(3)(a), and the largest paper size is 24 by 36 inches. Surveys must be on paper, and a non-paper survey adds a $5 per page paper copy fee. Liens must be notarized before you send them. Staff can't give legal advice or help fill out forms.

One rule catches people out: Denver cannot reject or refund a document recorded in the wrong county, so the person submitting it has to pick the right county.

When a loan is paid off or refinanced, the Public Trustee processes the release. The lender or title company files it, and the recorded release then appears in Denver's recorded document search.

You need three items: a signed and notarized Release of Deed of Trust, the deed of trust itself, and the original promissory note marked paid or cancelled. File electronically through Simplifile or Corporation Service Company, or mail by certified mail if you cannot.

An old loan that was paid years ago but never released can slow a closing. Ask the title company to search for unreleased deeds of trust at the start.

Clearing a recorded judgment takes steps in two offices:

  1. Mail the Acknowledgment of Satisfaction to the Denver District Court Clerk at 1437 Bannock St., Room 256, with a $20 certificate fee by cashier's check or money order and a stamped return envelope.
  2. Send the certificate to the Clerk and Recorder with the $43 recording fee and a self-addressed envelope.
  3. Send copies of the recorded certificate to the three credit bureaus, because the Recorder does not report to them.

A judgment lien left on record against a house will show up in the title search at closing.

sections.h2: What the recording step looks like at closing
sections.html:
At closing, the title company files the deed, the release of your old deed of trust and the buyer's paperwork, and each then appears in Denver's online recorded document database. Delays usually come from an unreleased deed of trust, a recorded judgment, a tax lien or, on an inherited house, a missing beneficiary deed or proof of death.

Fix these before listing, or before you accept an offer, and the closing date stays put. If you want a written cash offer on a Denver County house with a title problem, an unreleased loan or a tax balance, call us and we will look at it as is.

When a property secures a loan, the Public Trustee holds title in trust. Its two main jobs are running foreclosures, including auction sales when needed, and executing releases of deeds of trust so that paid-off mortgage liens come off the record. The office has a resource section for homeowners whose house sold at auction.

For a seller, the second job matters most. Your lender's release is what proves the old loan is gone, and the buyer's title insurer will want to see it recorded or in line to be recorded at closing.

A short checklist saves trouble later:

  1. Ask the title company to run a search on your address in Denver's recorded document database.
  2. Look for an unreleased deed of trust from a loan you paid off, a recorded judgment, a tax lien and, if you inherited the house, a beneficiary deed or proof of death.
  3. Start any release or satisfaction process right away, since the judgment steps involve two offices and mail time.
  4. Confirm the fee amounts if your closing falls near July 1.

Anything you clear before an offer arrives is one less item that can push your closing date.

If a problem does surface mid-sale, don't panic. Title companies deal with unreleased loans and old judgments all the time, and most can be resolved with a phone call to the lender or a filing like the ones described above. Just give the title officer the paperwork as soon as you have it.

A Colorado beneficiary deed is recorded with the Denver Clerk and Recorder, and it must be recorded before the owner dies. The statute requires recording in the county where the property sits, and the sample form warns in capitals that an unrecorded deed does not work (C.R.S. 15-15-404). The standard $43 recording fee applies. A revocation is also recorded with the clerk and recorder in the property's county under 15-15-405.

When a Denver owner has died and a buyer wants to purchase, the title company searches this same record for a beneficiary deed, a later revocation or any other recorded claim.

faqs.q: Where is the Denver County Clerk and Recorder?
faqs.a: The Recording Division is at 200 W. 14th Ave., Denver, CO 80204. In-person service requires an appointment, and mail and electronic submission are also available.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Denver?
faqs.a: $43 per document, plus the documentary fee of $0.10 per $1,000 on conveyances where it applies. Fees are scheduled to change on July 1, so confirm the current amount.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Denver?
faqs.a: Yes. The county recommends it and uses EPN and CSC as approved vendors. E-recording takes minutes, against 7 to 10 days for mail.

faqs.q: What is the fee for releasing a deed of trust in Denver?
faqs.a: $73 total, which covers the $43 recording fee and a $30 Public Trustee execution fee.

faqs.q: What happens if I record a deed in the wrong county?
faqs.a: Denver County cannot reject or refund a document recorded in the wrong county, so the person submitting it must pick the correct one.
